lead.en: Our species already lives in Africa, with faces like ours

summary.en: Skulls from the Moroccan cave of Jebel Irhoud are dated to about 300,000–315,000 years ago. Their faces are almost modern, while the braincase is still elongated. The find pushed the origin of our species back by 100,000 years and suggested it took shape across Africa rather than in one spot.

title.en: Denny, child of a Neanderthal and a Denisovan

lead.en: Her mother was a Neanderthal, her father a Denisovan

summary.en: A tiny bone fragment from Denisova Cave, picked out of 2,000 unidentified scraps, belonged to a girl of about 13 who lived some 90,000 years ago. Her genome showed a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father: the only first-generation hybrid of two human species ever found.

lead.en: Crosshatching in ochre, one of humanity's first signs

summary.en: On the South African coast, pieces of ochre scratched with a crosshatch and shell beads about 73,000–75,000 years old were found. They are among the oldest evidence of symbolic thought: people already adorned themselves and drew patterns that meant something.

lead.en: A small group leaves and goes on to people the world

summary.en: Some 70,000–50,000 years ago a small group of modern humans left Africa, probably across the narrow strait at the Red Sea when sea levels were lower. Nearly everyone in Eurasia, Australia and the Americas descends from them. Along the way they met Neanderthals and Denisovans, and traces of those meetings remain in our genes.

lead.en: Humans about a metre tall live on an Indonesian island

summary.en: In 2003 a cave on Flores yielded the skeleton of an adult about 1.1 metres tall. Nicknamed 'hobbits', Homo floresiensis lived on the island until modern humans arrived some 50,000 years ago, and probably shrank through island dwarfism, like many island animals.

lead.en: The first great sea voyage in human history

summary.en: Even with low sea levels, getting from Asia to Australia meant crossing tens of kilometres of open water. People did it at least 50,000 years ago, and by some datings of the Madjedbebe site as early as 65,000. The ancestors of Aboriginal Australians form one of the oldest continuous cultures on Earth.

lead.en: Ochre on the bones: Australia's oldest funeral rite

summary.en: On the shore of dried-up Lake Mungo, geologist Jim Bowler found in 1974 the skeleton of a man laid in a grave with folded hands and sprinkled with red ochre. By various estimates the burial is about 40,000 years old, one of the oldest ritual burials of Homo sapiens anywhere. In 2017 the remains were returned to the Aboriginal communities of the area.

lead.en: Our species' last close relatives fade from history

summary.en: Neanderthals lived in Europe and western Asia for hundreds of thousands of years, but vanished about 40,000 years ago. The causes are debated: competition with incoming sapiens, cold snaps, small numbers. They did not disappear without trace: about 2% of the genes of non-Africans today are Neanderthal.

lead.en: The world's oldest statue: a man with a lion's head

summary.en: Carved from mammoth ivory 35,000–41,000 years ago, this human figure with a cave lion's head is the oldest known statue. Found in pieces in 1939, it lay forgotten in the Ulm museum for some 30 years until an archaeologist assembled it from over 200 fragments.

lead.en: Lions and rhinos painted 8 times as long ago as the pyramids

summary.en: Hundreds of images of cave lions, rhinos, mammoths and horses were made about 36,000 years ago. The artists used perspective, shading and the rock's relief so the animals seemed to move by torchlight. The cave was only found in 1994; it is closed to visitors, and an exact replica stands nearby.

lead.en: More than 13,000 mammoth-ivory beads sewn on the dead

summary.en: At a site near Vladimir, burials about 34,000 years old were found: an adult man and two children in clothing sewn with more than 13,000 mammoth-ivory beads, with spears of straightened tusk. The beads alone took thousands of hours of work, so people already had rituals and perhaps inequality.

lead.en: Ice reaches Moscow and Chicago; seas sit 120 m lower

summary.en: About 26,000–19,000 years ago ice sheets covered Scandinavia, Britain and almost all of Canada. Sea level dropped by some 120 metres: Britain was part of the mainland, and a land bridge, Beringia, joined Chukotka and Alaska. People retreated to warmer refuges in southern Europe and Asia.

lead.en: People walk beside mammoths millennia 'too early'

summary.en: Dozens of human footprints by an ancient lake in New Mexico were dated, using seeds in the layers, to 21,000–23,000 years ago. If correct, people were in the Americas long before the 13,000–16,000 years once assumed; mammoth and giant sloth tracks lie nearby.

lead.en: Ochre mammoths and horses at the eastern edge of Ice Age Europe

summary.en: In Kapova Cave (Shulgan-Tash in Bashkir) in the Southern Urals, mammoths, horses, a woolly rhino, a bison, a Bactrian camel and geometric signs are painted in ochre. The images are at least 14,000–19,000 years old — the easternmost Ice Age cave art in Europe. Pyotr Rychkov described the cave in the 18th century, but the paintings were only noticed in 1959 by the zoologist Alexander Ryumin.

lead.en: A teenager's dog will find this Ice Age gallery

summary.en: The hundreds of bulls, horses and deer at Lascaux were painted 17,000–22,000 years ago, partly from scaffolds. The cave was found in 1940 by 18-year-old Marcel Ravidat, whose dog nosed into a hole under an uprooted tree; since 1963 visitors see only replicas.

lead.en: 18,000 years in the ice, fur and whiskers intact

summary.en: In 2018 a two-month-old puppy that died some 18,000 years ago was found in the Yakutian permafrost, fur and whiskers intact. DNA could not tell whether it was a dog or a wolf, so it was named Dogor, Yakut for 'friend'; in 2022 geneticists ruled it a wolf.

lead.en: Huts of 149 mammoth bones, found while digging a cellar

summary.en: In 1965 a farmer enlarging his cellar dug up a mammoth's jawbone. Archaeologists then uncovered four huts about 15,000 years old built from 149 mammoth bones, along with a mammoth skull painted with red ochre that is thought to have been a 'drum'.

lead.en: From Siberia across Beringia to the far south of Chile

summary.en: The ancestors of Native Americans came from Siberia across Beringia while it was still dry land. By about 14,500 years ago people were living at Monte Verde in southern Chile, 15,000 km from the strait. How they moved so fast, along the Pacific coast or through a corridor between ice sheets, is still debated.

lead.en: A sick puppy is nursed — and buried with its people

summary.en: Some 14,000 years ago a seven-month-old puppy was buried beside two people, one of the earliest secure records of the domestic dog. It had survived canine distemper, which researchers think was possible only because people fed, watered and cared for it.

lead.en: A stone sanctuary built by hunters, older than farming

summary.en: Rings of T-shaped pillars up to 5 metres tall, carved with foxes, boars and snakes, were raised around 9500 BC, before pottery, writing and apparently farming. The find upended the idea that fields and villages came first and temples later: it may have been the other way round.

lead.en: The world's oldest wooden sculpture, from the Urals

summary.en: Gold prospectors found the carved larch figure, covered with faces and patterns, in a peat bog in 1890. Radiocarbon dating in 2018 put it at about 11,500 years old, more than twice the age of the Egyptian pyramids and contemporary with Göbekli Tepe. It once stood over 5 metres tall and is now kept in Yekaterinburg.

lead.en: Wheat, barley and goats: people settle down

summary.en: Around 11,000 years ago people in the Fertile Crescent began sowing wheat and barley, and later tamed goats, sheep and cattle. Farming also arose independently in China, Mesoamerica, the Andes and New Guinea. Settled life brought population growth and villages, then cities, states and writing.

lead.en: Swimmers painted in the middle of the Sahara

summary.en: Rock paintings on the Gilf Kebir plateau show people apparently swimming, plus a giraffe and a hippo. They may date back to about 8000 BC, when the Sahara was green and wet; the shelter was found in 1933 by László Almásy, the real figure behind The English Patient.

lead.en: The oldest known boat: a dugout of Scots pine

summary.en: This three-metre canoe, hollowed out of a single Scots pine with flint or antler tools, is radiocarbon-dated to between 8040 and 7510 BC. It is the oldest known boat, made for hunters and fishers in a landscape of marshes, creeks and lakes.

lead.en: A cat buried with its owner 6,000 years before Egypt's cats

summary.en: At a Neolithic site on Cyprus, an eight-month-old cat was buried beside a human about 9,500 years ago. Cyprus had no wild cats, so the animal came by boat with people: the earliest known evidence of the bond between humans and cats.

lead.en: A town with no streets: people entered through the roof

summary.en: One of the largest Neolithic settlements: up to several thousand people in mud-brick houses packed wall to wall. There were no streets; people walked across the roofs and climbed down ladders inside. The walls bore paintings, and ancestors were buried under the floors.

lead.en: A weedy grass with tiny ears becomes the world's top grain

summary.en: About 9,000 years ago, farmers in southern Mexico began selecting seeds of teosinte, a wild grass whose ears held only a handful of kernels. Millennia of selection turned it into maize, which fed the Olmec, Maya, Aztecs and Inca. After Columbus it spread worldwide, and today it is the most-harvested grain on Earth.

title.en: The flutes and brew of Jiahu

lead.en: Crane-bone flutes still play after 9,000 years

summary.en: The Neolithic village of Jiahu yielded 33 flutes made from crane wing bones, up to 9,000 years old and among the oldest playable instruments. Its pottery held traces of a brew of rice, honey and hawthorn, a cross between beer, wine and mead.

lead.en: Britain becomes an island

summary.en: After the Ice Age a lived-in plain of rivers and marshes, Doggerland, lay where the North Sea is now. Melting ice raised the sea, and around 6200 BC a tsunami from the Storegga Slide off Norway apparently drowned what was left. Britain was cut off from the mainland for good.

lead.en: Teeth drilled in living people 9,000 years ago

summary.en: A Neolithic graveyard at Mehrgarh yielded eleven molars from nine adults with neat holes drilled while their owners were alive. The burials are 7,500–9,000 years old, making this the earliest evidence of a kind of proto-dentistry among early farmers.

lead.en: The oldest artificial mummies, 2,000 years before Egypt's

summary.en: Fishers of the Chinchorro culture began mummifying their dead around 5000 BC, roughly two millennia before the Egyptians. Bodies were taken apart, reinforced with sticks and reeds, coated in clay and given a mask. Everyone was preserved: the elderly, children, even unborn infants. The mummies became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021.

lead.en: Papuans invented farming on their own, with no outside help

summary.en: In a highland valley near Mount Hagen, archaeologists found traces of gardens: raised mounds and drainage ditches. By various estimates bananas, taro and yams were grown here about 7,000 years ago, and the first signs of cultivation go back some 3,000 years further. New Guinea is one of the few places where farming arose independently. Kuk has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2008.

lead.en: Channels in lava for farming eels, among the oldest aquaculture

summary.en: The Gunditjmara people cut channels, weirs and ponds into the hardened lava flows of the Budj Bim volcano to trap and raise eels. The oldest parts of the system are at least 6,600 years old, making it one of the world's oldest aquaculture systems. Stone house foundations survive nearby; the landscape was listed by UNESCO in 2019.

lead.en: The world's oldest worked gold, and its first rich men

summary.en: A Black Sea necropolis yielded some 3,000 gold objects about 6,500 years old, more than in the rest of the world from that time. Almost all of it lay in a few rich graves, making it one of the earliest signs of power and inequality of wealth.

lead.en: Wagons appear almost at once from Poland to Sumer

summary.en: Around 3500 BC wheeled wagons appear almost simultaneously in Mesopotamia, the Pontic steppe and Central Europe: a pot from Bronocice in Poland shows a wagon, and a wooden wheel with its axle about 5,150 years old was found in the Ljubljana Marshes. The potter's wheel probably came even before the wheel for transport.

lead.en: The oldest leather shoe is 5,500 years old — size 37

summary.en: In 2008 Armenia's Areni-1 cave produced a shoe cut from a single piece of hide, with laces and stuffed with grass: the oldest known leather footwear. It is roughly a European size 37, and the same cave later revealed the world's oldest known winery.

title.en: The horses of the Botai culture

lead.en: Early domestic horses — and maybe the 'wild' ones' ancestors

summary.en: Around 3500 BC the Botai people kept horses: their settlements hold vast numbers of horse bones, dung-filled pens and pots with traces of mare's milk. Genetics suggests that Przewalski's horses, long thought the last truly wild horses, descend from Botai stock.

lead.en: The first zoo, with hippos and elephants, before the pharaohs

summary.en: At Nekhen, one of Egypt's earliest capitals, archaeologists in 2009 found the burials of animals kept around 3500 BC: a leopard, crocodiles, hippos, elephants, baboons and cats. It is the oldest known menagerie, centuries before the first pharaohs.

lead.en: A walled city of dams and jade, one of China's first states

summary.en: In the Yangtze delta, around 3300–2300 BC, stood the walled city of Liangzhu, covering almost 3 km². Its people built a system of dams against floods and carved ritual jade bi discs and cong tubes. In 2019 the ruins were listed by UNESCO as evidence of an early state in China.

lead.en: Ice preserves a Copper Age man with all his gear

summary.en: A Copper Age man was killed by an arrow high in the Alps, and the ice preserved his body with clothing, a copper axe and a bow. Found in 1991, the mummy is a unique window on daily life in prehistoric Europe.

lead.en: Clay accounting tablets launch the age of writing

summary.en: Scribes in the Sumerian city of Uruk began recording accounts with signs on clay tablets, which evolved into cuneiform. One of the world's first writing systems, it shaped Near Eastern culture for three millennia.

title.en: Kushim, the first name in writing

lead.en: History's first written name belongs to a barley accountant

summary.en: Tablets from Uruk around 3200 BC bear the name Kushim, possibly the earliest recorded name of a person. All are accounts, such as '28,086 measures barley, 37 months, Kushim'; it is unclear whether this was an official, his title or an institution.

lead.en: Stone beds and dressers in a village older than the pyramids

summary.en: In the winter of 1850 a storm stripped the sand from a dune on Orkney, revealing a village lived in from about 3180 to 2500 BC. Each house has a hearth, stone beds on either side and a stone dresser facing the door, with drains running beneath.

lead.en: Two lands of the Nile merge — the age of pharaohs begins

summary.en: Narmer, a ruler of Upper Egypt, brought Upper and Lower Egypt under one crown, a victory shown on the famous Narmer Palette from Nekhen. It marks the start of the pharaonic state that lasted some three thousand years.

lead.en: A Neolithic sanctuary aligned with the solstice sun

summary.en: Neolithic Britons began a circular sanctuary on Salisbury Plain, raising its giant sarsen stones around 2500 BC. Aligned with the solstice sunrise and sunset, it is the most famous prehistoric monument in Europe.

lead.en: The savanna dries out and people head for the Nile

summary.en: For millennia the Sahara was a savanna of lakes, giraffes and hippos, as rock art records. By about 3000 BC, by most estimates, the humid period had ended in stages and people moved to the Nile, just as a unified Egyptian kingdom arose there.

lead.en: Giant sloths outlive their mainland kin by millennia

summary.en: Large ground sloths of the genus Megalocnus outlived their mainland relatives by thousands of years. According to the latest radiocarbon dates, they still lived on Cuba about 4,700 years ago, when Egypt was building its first pyramids.

lead.en: Imhotep builds the first monument entirely of cut stone

summary.en: The architect Imhotep built a six-stepped pyramid at Saqqara for Pharaoh Djoser. It is the earliest monumental building made entirely of cut stone and the prototype for all later Egyptian pyramids.

lead.en: One of the Americas' first cities, as old as the pyramids

summary.en: In Peru's Supe Valley, the city of Caral grew up with platform mounds and sunken plazas. Contemporary with Egypt's pyramids, it is one of the oldest cities in the Americas, built by a society without pottery or writing.

lead.en: A board game people kept playing for 4,500 years

summary.en: Leonard Woolley found boards for this 20-square game in the Royal Cemetery of Ur; they are some 4,500 years old. Its rules were rebuilt from a Babylonian tablet, and the game survived among the Jews of Kochi, India, until they emigrated to Israel in the 1950s.

lead.en: The world's tallest structure for nearly four millennia

summary.en: The Great Pyramid, built for Pharaoh Khufu at Giza, rose about 146 metres high. It remained the tallest human-made structure for nearly four millennia and is the only surviving Wonder of the Ancient World.

lead.en: The oldest papyrus: a logbook of stone for the pyramid

summary.en: Found on the Red Sea coast in 2013, the papyri of inspector Merer are the oldest inscribed papyri known, from Khufu's 26th year. Day by day, Merer logged how his crew shipped white limestone by boat from the Tura quarries to Giza, where the Great Pyramid was rising.

lead.en: A planned city with sewers — and a script still unread

summary.en: Mohenjo-daro became one of the largest cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation, with a grid of streets, brick houses, covered drains and the Great Bath. Its script remains undeciphered to this day.

title.en: Kerma, the first kingdom of Kush

lead.en: Nubia's first kingdom, a rival of Egypt, built of mud brick

place.en: Kerma, at the Third Cataract of the Nile (Sudan)

summary.en: Around 2500 BC the centre of the first Nubian state, the kingdom of Kush with its capital at Kerma, took shape at the Third Cataract of the Nile. Its huge mud-brick temple, the Western Deffufa, still stands, and royal mounds hold hundreds of people buried with the ruler. Around 1500 BC Kerma was conquered by the Egyptian pharaoh Thutmose I.

lead.en: A Syrian palace archive of 17,000 tablets, baked by fire

summary.en: In 1974–75 Paolo Matthiae's Italian team found some 17,000 clay tablets and fragments from the 24th century BC in the royal palace of Ebla. They hold accounts, treaties and Sumerian–Eblaite word lists. The fire that destroyed the palace baked the clay and preserved one of the world's oldest archives.

lead.en: Sumer conquered — a realm from the Gulf to the Mediterranean

summary.en: Sargon of Akkad conquered the city-states of Sumer and Akkad and built a realm stretching from the Persian Gulf toward the Mediterranean. Often called the first empire, it made Akkadian the lasting language of Mesopotamia.

lead.en: The first named author is a woman: Sargon's daughter

summary.en: Enheduanna, daughter of Sargon of Akkad, was high priestess of the moon god Nanna at Ur. Hymns to the goddess Inanna are attributed to her, so she is celebrated as the earliest known named author, though some scholars doubt the attribution.

title.en: The boy pharaoh's letter to Harkhuf

lead.en: A child pharaoh can't wait to see a pygmy

summary.en: Harkhuf of Elephantine led caravans deep into Nubia and brought back a pygmy from his last trip. The young Pepi II, king since age six, wrote that he would reward him richly if the pygmy arrived alive, and Harkhuf proudly carved the letter on his tomb.

lead.en: A century of drought some link to the fall of Akkad

summary.en: Around 2200 BC the climate from the Mediterranean to India turned sharply drier for about a century. The drought is linked, in a widely discussed but debated hypothesis, to the fall of the Akkadian Empire, the end of Egypt's Old Kingdom and the decline of Indus cities.

lead.en: Ur-Nammu raises a tower to the moon god in a Sumerian revival

summary.en: King Ur-Nammu, founder of the Third Dynasty of Ur, built a stepped temple tower to the moon god Nanna. It symbolised the Sumerian revival and is one of the best-preserved monuments of Mesopotamia.

title.en: Sintashta culture and the first chariots

lead.en: Spoked wheels — the invention that changed Eurasian warfare

summary.en: On the steppes of the southern Urals, the Sintashta people built fortified settlements and smelted bronze. Their graves hold the earliest known spoke-wheeled chariots, an invention that transformed warfare across Eurasia.

lead.en: The first king reigned for 28,800 years

summary.en: The list opens with kings who ruled before the Flood: the first, Alulim, reigned 28,800 years, and the eight antediluvian kings 241,200 years in all. After the Flood reigns 'shrank' to centuries, and Kish was ruled for 100 years by Kubaba, a tavern keeper.

lead.en: By tradition, China's first dynasty, founded by Yu the Great

summary.en: Chinese tradition holds that Yu the Great founded the Xia, the first dynasty. Its historicity is debated, but many scholars link it to the Erlitou culture on the Yellow River, one of China's earliest states.

lead.en: Mammoths still roam while the pyramids are centuries old

summary.en: Woolly mammoths died out on the mainland about 10,000 years ago, but an isolated population on Wrangel Island survived, according to the latest finds, until about 2000 BC. By then the pyramids of Giza had already stood for centuries.

lead.en: A 4,000-year-old bowl of noodles

summary.en: In 2005 thin yellow strands were found in an upturned pot at Lajia on the Yellow River: the oldest known noodles, about 4,000 years old. Mudflows buried the village; since millet alone cannot form noodles, other starches were probably mixed in.

lead.en: Bigger than Pompeii's blast, yet Bronze Age villagers escape

summary.en: Long before Pompeii, Vesuvius produced an even larger eruption, estimated at around 1995 BC (dates vary by centuries). Bronze Age villagers managed to flee: thousands of their footprints are preserved in the ash.

lead.en: A Yellow River megaflood that may lie behind China's flood myth

summary.en: Geologists found traces of a catastrophic Yellow River flood, dated to about 1920 BC, when a landslide dam burst. Some scholars see it as the origin of the legend of the Great Flood and Yu the Great; others dispute the link.

lead.en: Heart of the Minoans, Europe's first advanced civilization

summary.en: The first palace at Knossos was built on Crete as the heart of Minoan civilisation, Europe's first advanced culture. Its maze of halls, frescoes and plumbing later inspired the Greek myth of the Labyrinth and the Minotaur.

lead.en: Babylon carves a 282-law code into basalt

summary.en: King Hammurabi of Babylon had 282 laws on trade, family, property and punishment carved on a basalt stele. It is one of the oldest and most complete written legal codes in history.

lead.en: The oldest customer complaint: bad copper

summary.en: A man named Nanni berates the Ur merchant Ea-nasir: the Dilmun copper was poor, his servant was treated rudely and his money was not refunded. Leonard Woolley found it among other complaints about the same trader; Guinness calls it the oldest customer complaint.

lead.en: Hunter-gatherers raise giant earthworks without farming

summary.en: In the lower Mississippi Valley, hunter-gatherers raised a vast complex of concentric earthen ridges and mounds. It is one of the largest monuments of its age in North America, built without farming.

lead.en: A volcano tears the island apart and buries Akrotiri in ash

summary.en: One of the largest eruptions of recent millennia blew apart the island of Thera and buried the town of Akrotiri in ash. Its date is debated: radiocarbon suggests about 1600 BC, archaeology nearer 1500 BC. It is sometimes linked to the Atlantis myth.

lead.en: China's first dynasty confirmed by archaeology

summary.en: According to tradition, Tang of Shang overthrew the last Xia ruler and founded the Shang dynasty. It is the first Chinese dynasty confirmed by archaeology, known for bronze casting, walled cities and chariots.

title.en: The rubber balls of El Manatí

lead.en: The oldest rubber balls lie in an Olmec sacred bog

summary.en: Around 1600–1200 BC the Olmecs left offerings in the bog of El Manatí: wooden busts, axes and rubber balls. The muck preserved them remarkably well; the balls are the oldest rubber objects known and were probably used in the Mesoamerican ballgame.

lead.en: The oldest picture of the sky, dug up by looters

summary.en: This bronze disc with a gold sun or moon, crescent and stars, probably including the Pleiades, is the oldest known concrete depiction of the heavens. Treasure hunters with a metal detector dug it up and sold it in 1999; in 2002 a police sting in Basel recovered it.

lead.en: Mursili I's raid ends the dynasty of Hammurabi

summary.en: The Hittite king Mursili I led a long raid down the Euphrates and sacked Babylon. The First Dynasty of Babylon, Hammurabi's line, fell, and the Kassites ruled Mesopotamia for four centuries. By the 'middle chronology' the raid is dated to 1595 BC.

lead.en: Pottery-making seafarers set out to settle Oceania

summary.en: Seafarers of the Lapita culture, known for their stamped pottery, appeared in the Bismarck Archipelago. Their descendants sailed canoes to settle remote Oceania: Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa.

lead.en: Hymns to the gods become Hinduism's oldest text

summary.en: In north-western India, Vedic Aryans began composing Sanskrit hymns to their gods, later gathered as the Rigveda. Passed down orally for centuries, it is the oldest scripture of Hinduism and a key Indo-European text.

lead.en: Rice and millet fields lure jungle fowl into human company

summary.en: According to recent research, the earliest securely dated domestic chicken bones come from Thailand, around 1650–1250 BC. Red junglefowl were probably drawn to rice and millet fields, at the time Egypt's New Kingdom pharaohs ruled.

lead.en: Ships sail the Red Sea for incense, gold and ebony

summary.en: Queen-pharaoh Hatshepsut sent ships down the Red Sea to the land of Punt for incense, gold and ebony. Reliefs in her temple at Deir el-Bahari are among the earliest depictions of an overseas trading voyage.

lead.en: Egypt takes the Levant in the first battle recorded in detail

summary.en: Pharaoh Thutmose III defeated a coalition of Canaanite kings and took Megiddo after a siege, securing Egyptian power in the Levant. It is the first battle recorded in detail in historical sources.

lead.en: Seafarers from Southeast Asia bring dogs to the continent

summary.en: The oldest known dingo remains, found in Western Australia, date to about 3,450 years ago. The dogs were brought by sea by people from Southeast Asia, though exactly who they were remains unknown.

title.en: The Hurrian hymn, oldest written music

lead.en: A 3,400-year-old song with its notation nearly complete

summary.en: The royal palace of Ugarit held about 36 hymns written in cuneiform around 1400 BC, complete with musical instructions. The hymn to the goddess Nikkal survives nearly whole, making it the oldest substantially complete work of notated music known.

lead.en: Buried in summer 1370 BC, in a short corded skirt

summary.en: Tree rings in her oak coffin show the girl, aged 16–18, was buried in the summer of 1370 BC, with a yarrow flower laid on the lid. She wore a wool blouse and a knee-length corded skirt, beside a birch-bark pail of drink made from wheat, honey and cowberries.

lead.en: A pharaoh raises the sun disk above all other gods

summary.en: Pharaoh Akhenaten elevated the sun disc Aten above all other gods and built a new capital, Akhetaten. His reform transformed Egyptian art but was reversed after his death and the city abandoned.

lead.en: The pharaoh's blade was forged from fallen sky-iron

summary.en: Iron was a rarity in the Bronze Age, and the dagger from Tutankhamun's tomb was made from a meteorite: its blade holds 11% nickel and 0.6% cobalt. Iron smelted from terrestrial ores before the 19th century never contains more than 4% nickel.

lead.en: Ten tonnes of copper and Nefertiti's scarab on the seabed

summary.en: In 1982 a sponge diver sketched 'metal biscuits with ears' he had seen on the seabed off Cape Uluburun: copper ingots. The ship, wrecked in the late 14th century BC, carried ten tonnes of copper in 354 ingots and a gold scarab bearing Nefertiti's name.

lead.en: A chariot stalemate leads to one of the first peace treaties

summary.en: The armies of Ramesses II and the Hittite king Muwatalli II clashed at Kadesh in perhaps the largest chariot battle ever fought. It ended inconclusively and later led to one of the earliest known peace treaties.

lead.en: Ramesses II's colossi, later moved to escape the Aswan Dam

summary.en: Ramesses II, who ruled Egypt for 66 years, had two temples with colossal statues of himself carved into a Nubian cliff. In the 1960s they were cut into blocks and moved uphill to escape the Aswan Dam reservoir in a landmark UNESCO rescue.

lead.en: Questions to the ancestors — the oldest Chinese writing

summary.en: At the Shang capital of Yin under King Wu Ding, diviners carved questions to the ancestors on turtle shells and ox bones. These are the earliest known Chinese writing, the direct ancestor of modern characters.

lead.en: In the Bible, Moses leads Israel out of slavery

summary.en: The biblical narrative tells how Moses led the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt and received the Ten Commandments on Mount Sinai. The Exodus is not confirmed by archaeology, but it became the founding story of Judaism and of Passover.

lead.en: Colossal stone heads from Mesoamerica's mother culture

summary.en: On the Gulf Coast of Mexico, San Lorenzo became the first great Olmec centre, famed for its colossal stone heads. The Olmecs are often called the 'mother culture' of later Mesoamerican civilisations.

lead.en: Giant masks show early China was more than one civilization

summary.en: In Sichuan, the distinctive Sanxingdui culture cast huge bronze masks and statues unlike anything from the Shang. Its finds showed that early China was not a single Yellow River civilisation.

lead.en: Gone from the mainland, it survives only in Tasmania

summary.en: The thylacine is estimated to have died out on mainland Australia about 3,200 years ago, close to the Late Bronze Age collapse in the Mediterranean. A drier climate, humans and possibly dingoes are blamed; in Tasmania it survived into the 20th century.

lead.en: A royal wife who led armies: the 'Chinese Tutankhamun'

summary.en: One of the many wives of the Shang king Wu Ding, Fu Hao was a general and high priestess whose campaigns are recorded on oracle bones. Her tomb, found intact in 1976 with weapons and over 700 jades, earned her the name 'the Chinese Tutankhamun'.

lead.en: Legend tells of a ten-year siege ended by a wooden horse

summary.en: According to legend, the Achaeans under Agamemnon besieged Troy for ten years and took it with the wooden horse; Eratosthenes dated its fall to 1184 BC. Excavations at Hisarlik show that the city was indeed destroyed around that time.

title.en: Ramesses III repels the Sea Peoples

lead.en: Egypt holds firm as the Bronze Age world collapses

summary.en: Pharaoh Ramesses III defeated the fleet of the Sea Peoples, who had ravaged the Hittite kingdom and Levantine cities. Egypt survived, but the invasions were part of the Late Bronze Age collapse in the eastern Mediterranean.

lead.en: 'We are hungry!': the first recorded strike

summary.en: Around Ramesses III's 25th year, the royal tomb builders of Deir el-Medina downed tools and walked off the job: their wheat rations were late, 'eighteen days have passed this month'. The authorities heard them and work resumed next day, but more strikes followed.

lead.en: 22 letters that gave rise to Greek, Latin and Cyrillic

summary.en: The Phoenicians spread a 22-letter consonantal alphabet, attested on King Ahiram's sarcophagus at Byblos. It gave rise to the Greek and Aramaic scripts, and through them to Latin, Cyrillic, Hebrew and Arabic.

lead.en: Shang falls and the Mandate of Heaven is born

summary.en: King Wu of Zhou defeated the army of Di Xin, the last Shang king, and founded the Zhou dynasty. The victory was justified by the 'Mandate of Heaven', an idea that underpinned Chinese politics for three millennia.
